Nhưng tôi quản lĩnh quân áo đen, chúng nó còn có từ tâm, chứ họ Đinh quản lĩnh quân áo trắng, phần nhiều là những tên ác quỷ, bác không nên không lo liệu trước.

Lê hỏi:

- Vậy thì làm thế nào?

Dĩ Thành nói:

- Mỗi một soái bộ đêm sai hàng hơn một nghìn tên quân, chia đi làm ôn dịch các nơi. Bác nên sắm nhiều cỗ bàn bày sẵn ở sân. Bọn chúng từ xa đến tất là đói khát, thấy cỗ liền ăn mà không suy nghĩ gì. Bác núp ở một chỗ tối, đợi khi thấy ăn uống gần xong, bấy giờ mới ra sụp lạy, nhưng cũng đừng kêu nài gì cả. Như thế họa may có cứu vãn được phần nào chăng.

Đoạn rồi ứa nước mắt cùng nhau từ biệt.

Lê Ngộ về quê nhà, thì bệnh dịch đương nổi rất dữ, vợ con đều mắc rất nặng, hầu không thể nhận được nhau nữa. Bèn theo lời Dĩ Thành, đêm hôm ấy làm cỗ rất hậu bầy ra sân. Quả thấy có đám đông quỷ sứ từ trên không bay đến nhìn nhau mà nói:

- Chúng ta đều đói cả, sẵn cỗ đây không ăn thì còn đi đâu. Chả lẽ vì uống mấy chén rượu mà đã đến phải tội được.

Chúng bèn cùng quây lại đánh chén. Một người mặc áo tía chễm chệ ngồi chính giữa, còn những người khác đều đứng chầu chung quanh, kẻ cầm dao búa, người cầm sổ sách. Thấy họ ăn uống gần xong, Lê Ngộ ra lạy mãi, lạy mãi. Người áo tía nói:

- Ta đương đánh chén, gã kia đến đây làm gì?

Chúng quỷ nói:

- Chắc là người chủ bày những mâm cỗ này, nhà hắn có người ốm nặng, kêu xin châm chước.

Người áo tía tức giận, cầm quyển sổ ném xuống đất mà nói:

- Lẽ đâu vì cho mâm cỗ sơ sài mà đánh đổi được năm mạng người hay sao!

Chúng quỷ nói:

- Nhưng đã ăn của nhà nó, chả lẽ nỡ làm ngơ không cứu. Thôi thì dù có vì cứu nó mà phải tội, dẫu chết ta cũng bằng lòng.

Người áo tía ngẫm nghĩ một lúc lâu, bèn lấy bút son xóa bỏ hơn mười chữ rồi đi. Sau vài ngày, nhà họ Lê ai nấy đều khỏi cả. Lê cảm ân đức của Dĩ Thành, bèn lập miếu ở nhà để thờ. Người làng đến khấn vái kêu cầu cũng thường ứng nghiệm.

Lời bình:

Than ôi! Bè bạn là một ở trong năm đạo thường, có thể coi khinh ư? Câu chuyện quỷ Dạ Xoa này, thật có hay không, không cần phải biện luận cho lắm. Chỉ có một điều đáng nói là sự giao du của Dĩ Thành, khi đã coi ai làm người bạn chân chính thì sống chết không đổi thay, hoạn nạn cùng cứu gỡ. Đời những kẻ kết bạn ở chung quanh mâm rượu, gan dạ đảo điên, hễ lâm đến sự lợi hại thì lờ đi như không biết nhau, nghe chuyện này há chẳng chạnh lòng hổ thẹn sao!

Chú thích:

(1) Quốc Oai: nay thuộc tỉnh Hà Tây, Hiện ở làng gối huyện Đan Phượng còn có đền thờ Văn Dĩ Thành.

(2) Trần Trùng Quang tên là Quý Khoáng, lãnh đạo cuộc khởi nghĩa chống quân Minh từ 1409-1413, cuộc khởi nghĩa bị dập tắt, Trùng Quang bị bắt và bị giết. Cũng như Trần Giản Định ông được quốc sử coi là nhà Hậu Trần.

(3) Nhan Hồi là học trò Khổng Tử, được coi là bậc đại hiền, khi mất mới 32 tuổi. Đời Tấn, Tô Thiều đã chết lại hồi, người em là Tiết hỏi chuyện; Thiều nói thấy hai ông Nhan Hồi và Bốc Thương làm chức Tu văn lang ở dưới đất.

(4) Theo nguyên chú, Lý Hạ tự là Trương Cát làm văn rất lanh, đặt bút là thành. Một hôm thấy một người cầm một cái thẻ chữ viết như lối chữ triện cổ, đến bảo Thượng đế mới làm xong cái lầu Bạch Ngọc, vời thầy lên làm cho bài ký. Không bao lâu thì Hạ chết. Từ đấy khi nói về văn nhân mất sớm, người ta thường nói là "ngọc lâu phó triệu".

(5) Quế Dương: nay thuộc tỉnh Bắc Ninh.

(6) Theo nguyên chú vua Hán Văn Đế yêu quý người bầy tôi là Đăng Thông, thấy thầy tướng bảo Thông sẽ phải chết đói, bèn cho cả núi đồng ở đất Thục, cho được phép đúc tiền mà tiêu, sẽ không còn lo chết đói nữa. Nhưng sau Văn đế mất, Cảnh Đế lên làm vua, ghét Thông, tịch thu cả gia sản. Thông phải đi ở nhờ và quả nhiên chết đói.

(7) Theo nguyên chú, Chu Thù nhà nghèo, chiêm bao thấy Thượng đế thương mình. Ngài hỏi vị thần tư mệnh: Nó có giàu được không? Tư mệnh nói: Số nó nghèo lắm. Nhưng hiện có số tiền của thằng Xe, có thể cho nó mượn được, rồi đến kỳ thằng Xe nó sinh, thì lại phải trả. Sau Chu khá giàu: đúng đến kỳ hạn, Chu xe tiền của chạy đi trốn. Buổi tối Chu dừng xe nghỉ ở dọc đường, gặp một người đàn bà chửa xin tạm nằm nhờ ở dưới xe. Đêm ấy người đàn bà đẻ đứa con trai; vì nghĩ nó đẻ ở dưới xe, bèn đặt tên là thằng Xe. Từ đấy Chu làm gì cũng thất bại, lại thành nghèo kiết.

(8) Vương Bột đời Đường theo cha đi làm quan, đậu thuyền ở dưới núi Mã Đương, mộng thấy vua Thủy phủ giúp cho một trận gió. Hôm sau quả nhiên có gió thuận, thuyền đến Nam Xương, làm bài Tựa Đằng vương các.

(9) Phạm Trọng Yêm đời Tống khi làm trấn thủ Nhiêu Chân, có người học trò vào yết kiến, nói tình cảnh đói rét nghèo khổ. Bấy giờ người ta đương mộ lối chữ đẹp của Âu Dương Suất Canh viết khắc ở tấm bia chùa Tiến Phúc. Ông Phạm bèn mua giấy mực định cấp cho người học trò ấy đến chùa rập lấy nghìn bản rồi đến kinh mà bán lấy tiền. Người học trò chưa kịp đến rập, bỗng một hôm mưa gió, tấm bia bị sét đánh vỡ mất. Vì vậy có câu thơ: Thời lai phong tống Đằng vương các, Vận khứ lôi oanh Tiến Phúc bi (Gặp thời gió đẩy tới Gác Đằng vương; Vận rủi sét đánh tan bia Tiến Phúc).

(10) Nhan Uyên, Mẫu Tử Khiên đều là học trò đức hạnh của Khổng Tử.

(11) Lư Chiếu Lân và Lạc Tân Vương là hai danh sĩ đời Đường Cao Tông. Bùi Hành Kiệm thường chê là những người nóng nảy xốc nổi, không phải là kiểu người được hưởng tước lộc. Sau Lư vì ác tật mà gieo mình xuống nước chết, Lạc thì vì dự vào đảng loạn phải chết, đúng như lời Kiệm nói.

(12) Trường Giang: ở đây có lẽ chỉ sông Hồng.

en.title: Chapter 20: The Tale of the Yaksha General
en.html:
In the district of Quoc Oai there lived a man of rare and singular spirit, Van Di Thanh by name (1), bold and chivalrous by nature, who would never let himself be beguiled by ghosts or demons. Flower demons and moon fiends, lewd gods and baleful spirits that had no place in the register of sanctioned rites, he held in contempt and did not fear in the least. Toward the close of the Trung Quang reign of the Tran dynasty (2), the dead were beyond counting, and wronged souls with no place to rest gathered together in packs and droves. Some knocked at the doors of eating-houses to beg a morsel, while others waylaid young women out roaming abroad to form fleeting unions. Whoever crossed them fell gravely ill, and whoever made offerings to them found them wondrously potent. So they ran rampant across the fields and countryside, fearing nothing and heeding no one. One day Di Thanh, flushed with wine, rode out among them on horseback, and the ghosts and demons scattered in terror. He quickly called after them:

"You were all men of valor who met with misfortune. I have come to visit you, wishing to set before you what serves your interest and what harms it. I beg you, do not shun me so."

Little by little the ghosts gathered again and invited him to take the seat of honor. Di Thanh then reasoned with them:

"You delight in bringing calamity upon people and in sending them to their deaths. Pray tell, to what end?"

They answered:

"We wish to swell our ranks."

Di Thanh said:

"You wish to swell your ranks, yet what of the harm you do the living? The more soldiers you have, the scarcer your food and drink must grow. The fewer the living, the thinner the offerings made to you. What profit is there for you in it, that you persist in such deeds? Let loose your desires, and all the gullies and streams could not fill them. Give rein to your wickedness, and even tigers and wolves seem gentle beside you. So long as it profits you, you will not refuse even a scrap of cloth or a slip of paper. So long as it fills your bellies, you are not ashamed to scrape at shattered pots and broken dishes. You toil and grub after jars and bottles, and scramble eagerly for gruel and rice. Sowing calamity and scattering misfortune, you usurp the authority of the Creator. Shrieking from the rooftops and peering into bedchambers, you trouble the hearts of the common folk. You take pleasure in all this, but I am ashamed of it. Moreover, Heaven rules by virtue and not by terror, and men cherish life and do not love slaughter. Yet you presume to deal out fortune and calamity as you please, giving free rein to arrogance and excess. The Lord on High will not suffer it, and punishment will surely come. Where, then, will you flee to escape being put to the sword?"

The ghosts, stricken with sorrow, replied:

"We do this not by choice but because we must. In life we never found our season, and in death we went before our appointed hour. When we hunger, no one feeds us. When we retreat, we have nowhere to shelter. Amid mounds of white bones the grass and moss grieve, and upon drifts of yellow sand the frost and wind blow bitter cold. So we cannot help but gather our fellows and scrape together what morsels we may. What is more, that household's fortunes are about to turn, and it will soon be ruined and scattered. That is why the Underworld Court has not forbidden us, for we have already made our petition. We fear that next year will be worse still than this one."

Then the kitchen brought out a feast, and platters and dishes crowded the tables. When the scholar asked where it had come from, he learned that the meat was an ox seized from one village and the wine a basket of fermented mash taken from another. He ate and drank with tremendous speed, sweeping through the food like wind and rain. The ghosts rejoiced and said to one another:

"Truly, this is our commander!"

Then they said to the scholar:

"We are a motley rabble, each of us playing chieftain for himself. With no one to lead us all, we cannot last for long. Now Your Excellency has favored us by coming here. It is Heaven that has given Your Excellency to us."

Di Thanh said:

"I am versed in both letters and arms, and humble though I am, I could serve as a general. But the world of the living and the world of the dead lie apart. What would become of my aged mother?"

The ghosts said:

"Not so. We ask only that Your Excellency keep your dignity and issue your commands. By day we shall scatter to our separate quarters, and by night we shall send an officer to report to you. We would not dare trouble you to go down to the Nine Springs."

Di Thanh said:

"If I must be pressed into your service, I have six rules of conduct. You must swear to obey them."

They all agreed, and asked him to come to that place on the third night to raise an altar. When the night came, all the ghosts assembled. One old ghost arrived late, and the scholar ordered him beheaded. Every one of them trembled with fear. The scholar then gave his orders:

"You shall not hold my commands in contempt. You shall not indulge in lewd ways. You shall not make mischief that costs the people their lives. You shall not plunder, and you must rescue the people in their troubles. By day you shall not take on false forms, and by night you shall not band together. Obey my commands, and I shall be your general. Defy them, and I shall punish you for your crimes. Mark my words well, lest you live to regret it."

He then divided them into companies and squads, and ordered that whenever anything good or ill occurred, they must come and report it to him.

More than a month passed in this way. One day, as Di Thanh sat at his leisure, a man appeared who called himself an envoy of the Underworld Court and asked him to come away. Di Thanh was about to put him off when the man said:

"This is the command of King Yama. His Majesty sees that you are a man of firm resolve and means to grant you rank and office. No harm will come to you, so do not refuse. I will, however, give you a generous span of time. You shall come of your own accord, and I shall wait for you along the road."

With these words he vanished. Di Thanh summoned the ghosts and questioned them, and they all answered:

"It is true, my lord. We had not yet found the moment to tell you. King Yama, seeing of late that the world of the living had fallen upon troubled times, created four Yaksha divisions. Each is led by a general who holds the power to punish and to slay and who is entrusted with the lives of all living beings. The burden is a heavy one, unlike that of any other office. Your lordship's renown is great, and His Majesty has already heard of you. We, too, have recommended you with all our hearts, and so he means to appoint you to this high post."

Di Thanh said:

"If what you say is so, is this a blessing or a curse for me?"

"In the court of King Yama, men are chosen no differently than Buddhas are. No bribe can buy a post, and no stroke of luck can win one. A man who keeps himself upright will be raised up, however humble he may be. A man whose conduct is crooked will be passed over, however exalted his rank. The task of training and commanding these troops belongs to you, my lord, and to no one else. If you linger over your wife and children and let the days and months slip by, the post will fall into another man's hands, and we too shall grieve."

Di Thanh clicked his tongue and said:

"Death is a hateful thing, yet a good name cannot be bought. Moreover, the brush that is sharpest soonest wears dull, and the pine is felled for the sake of its fine boughs. Were it not for its splendid plumage, why should the pheasant court disaster? Were it not for its white tusks, why should the elephant be burned? Are the swan goose and the wild goose not slaughtered precisely because they cannot cry out? The ailanthus and the gnarled oak live long only because they are worthless. Yan Hui was but thirty-two when he was summoned to serve as a scribe beneath the earth (3). Li He was scarcely twenty-seven when he was called to write a record for a tower in heaven (4). A man born into this world, if he cannot wear gold at his girdle and tread the jade halls of office, should at least leave a name that endures ten thousand ages. Why should I keep my head bowed in this muddied world, haggling over whether my life is long or short?"

He put his household affairs in order, and then he died.

At that time a man of his village named Le Ngo, who had long been a close friend of Di Thanh, was wandering in the region of Que Duong (5) and lodging at an inn. One night, a little after the first watch, Le Ngo saw a man arrive on a fine steed with a bustling train of attendants and servants and ask to see him. The innkeeper lifted the bamboo blind to welcome him. Le Ngo was astonished that the guest's voice sounded just like Di Thanh's, though his face bore only a faint resemblance to his friend's. Le Ngo was about to slip out the door to avoid him when the guest spoke:

"Your old friend knows you. How is it that you do not know your old friend?"

He then gave his home village and his name. He said that he had been granted high office in the underworld and that, for the sake of their old friendship, he had come to visit Le Ngo.

Then he took off his fur coat and pawned it with the innkeeper for wine so that they could drink and make merry. After several rounds, Le seized the moment and said:

"All my life I have striven to build up hidden merit. I have never schemed for my own gain, nor brought peril upon others. In teaching, I have guided each pupil according to his gifts; in my own studies, I have toiled with every ounce of my strength. I have not chased idle dreams, nor gone beyond what is proper. Why, then, must I scratch out a living in every corner of the land and lean on strangers in my solitude? My children cry with empty bellies, and my wife laments the cold that chills her to the bone. At home I lack even a hut to keep out the wind, and on the road I have not so much as a hat against the rain. East and west, I wander without end. Meanwhile, many of my friends have risen to office. In talent and learning we are equals, yet our stations and our names lie worlds apart. Why should one man live in comfort while another suffers so?"

Di Thanh replied:

"Wealth and rank cannot be sought, and poverty is a matter of fate. So it was that Deng Tong owned a mountain of copper yet starved to death (6), and the boy Chezi's fortune sat for a time in Zhou's treasury (7). When fate is kind, the wind carries a man's boat past Mount Madang (8). When fate is unkind, lightning strikes the Jianfu stele (9). Were it otherwise, men as virtuous as Yan and Min (10) would surely have ascended to high office, and why would poets as gifted as Luo and Lu (11) have remained humble commoners all their lives? What comes about without our doing is Heaven's will, and what arrives without our calling is fate. What makes a scholar worthy is only this: to stay poor without fawning, to stay steadfast in hardship, to do the work his station asks of him and accept what his lot brings. As for success and failure, glory and disgrace, what power have we to bend them to our will?"

When the wine was gone, they trimmed the lamp and talked on together, and the more they talked, the less they tired of it. The next day, as they were about to part, Di Thanh sent everyone else out of the room and said:

"I have just received a decree from the Lord on High, charging me also with command of the hosts of plague spirits. They will be sent out to do their work across every prefecture and district. Famine and war will follow, and the people will be so ravaged that only four or five in ten will survive. Anyone without deep stores of blessing will likely perish, jade and common stone shattered alike. Your household's blessings are thin, and I fear you cannot escape. You should go home to your native village soon, and not linger any longer in a strange land."

Le said:

"But I thought I might count on you to shelter me?"

Di Thanh replied:

"It lies outside my domain, and I cannot overstep its bounds. North of the Truong Giang (12) is under my command, but west of the Truong Giang is in the keeping of a general named Dinh. The troops I lead wear black, and they still have some mercy in them. But the troops under Dinh wear white, and most of them are wicked demons. You would do well to make your preparations now."

Le asked:

"Then what am I to do?"

Di Thanh replied:

"Each commander's division sends out more than a thousand soldiers every night, dispersed to spread pestilence across the land. You should prepare an abundant feast and set it out in your courtyard. Having come from afar, they are sure to be hungry and thirsty, and at the sight of the food they will eat without a second thought. Hide yourself somewhere in the shadows, and when you see that they have nearly finished eating and drinking, only then come forth and prostrate yourself before them. Yet do not plead for anything at all. In this way, perhaps, some part of the calamity may yet be averted."

With that, tears welling in their eyes, the two friends bade each other farewell.

When Le Ngo returned to his native village, the pestilence was raging fiercely. His wife and children had all fallen gravely ill, so stricken that they could scarcely recognize one another. Following Di Thanh's counsel, that very night he prepared a lavish feast and laid it out in the courtyard. Just as foretold, a great throng of demon minions came flying down from the sky. They looked at one another and said:

"We are all hungry. Here is a feast laid out and waiting. If we don't eat it, where else would we go? Surely a few cups of wine cannot bring punishment down upon us."

So they gathered round and fell to eating and drinking. A figure in purple robes sat imposingly at the center, while the others stood in attendance around him, some holding knives and axes, others carrying ledgers and registers. When he saw that they had nearly finished, Le Ngo came forth and bowed before them over and over. The one in purple said:

"I am in the midst of my feast. What does that fellow want here?"

The demons replied:

"He must be the master of the house who laid out this feast. Someone in his household is gravely ill, and he has come to beg for leniency."

The one in purple flew into a rage. He flung a ledger to the ground and said:

"Can a paltry meal truly buy back five human lives?"

The demons said:

"Yet we have already eaten from his household. How could we have the heart to turn a blind eye to his plight? Should saving him bring punishment upon us, we would accept it gladly, though it cost us our lives."

The one in purple pondered for a long while. At last he took up a vermilion brush, struck out more than ten characters, and departed. Within a few days, every member of the Le household had recovered. Grateful for Di Thanh's kindness, Le built a shrine in his home to worship him. The villagers, too, came there to offer prayers and petitions, and these were often answered.

Critique

Alas! Friendship is one of the Five Constant Relationships. How could it ever be taken lightly? Whether this tale of the Yaksha is true or not need not be argued at length. One thing alone deserves mention: how steadfastly Di Thanh kept faith in friendship. Once he deemed a man his true friend, neither life nor death could alter his devotion, and in times of peril he never failed to come to his aid. As for those in this world who make friends over cups of wine, their hearts ever shifting, and who feign not to know one another the moment profit or peril is at stake, how could they hear this tale and not blush with shame?

Notes

  • (*) Original title: Da Xoa Bo Soai Luc (Yasha Boshuai Lu — Record of the Yaksha General).
  • (1) Quoc Oai and Van Di Thanh: Quoc Oai is now a district of Hanoi (formerly part of Ha Tay Province). In Goi Village (Thuong Hoi), Dan Phuong District, a temple dedicated to Van Di Thanh still stands today.
  • (2) Trung Quang reign: Tran Trung Quang, whose personal name was Quy Khoang, led the resistance against the Ming armies from 1409 to 1413. When the uprising was crushed, Trung Quang was captured and perished on the way to China. Alongside Tran Gian Dinh, he is counted by national histories as a sovereign of the Later Tran dynasty.
  • (3) Yan Hui serving as a scribe beneath the earth: Yan Hui, Confucius's foremost disciple, died at only thirty-two. During the Jin dynasty, Su Shao died and returned to life; when his younger brother Su Jie asked him about the netherworld, Shao said he had seen Yan Hui and Bu Shang serving as Officers of Literary Compilation in the underworld. See also Note (8) to Chapter 10, The Tale of Pham Tu Hu's Journey to the Celestial Court.
  • (4) Li He called to write a record in heaven: According to the original annotation, the Tang poet Li He (courtesy name Changji) wrote with extraordinary speed and brilliance. When he was twenty-seven, a man in crimson robes appeared to him riding a hornless red dragon and carrying a tablet inscribed in ancient seal script. He announced that the Lord on High had just finished building the White Jade Tower (Baiyulou) and was summoning Li He to write a commemorative record for it; shortly afterward, Li He died. Ever since, a man of letters who dies young is spoken of as having "answered the summons to the Jade Tower."
  • (5) Que Duong: Now part of Bac Ninh Province.
  • (6) Deng Tong: According to the original annotation, Emperor Wen of Han dearly favored his courtier Deng Tong. When a physiognomist predicted that Tong would die of starvation, the emperor granted him an entire copper mountain in the land of Shu, with permission to mint coins for his own use so that he would never starve. After Emperor Wen died, however, Emperor Jing ascended the throne, dismissed Tong, and confiscated all his wealth; reduced to depending on the charity of others, Deng Tong indeed starved to death.
  • (7) Chezi ("Cart Boy") and Zhou's treasury: According to the original annotation, Zhou Shu (also recorded as Zhanguri/Zhou) was a poor man who dreamed that the Lord on High took pity on him and asked the Arbiter of Fate, "Can this man become rich?" The god replied, "He is fated to be poor. However, there is wealth in the treasury set aside for a boy named Chezi ('Cart Boy'), who has not yet been born; it may be lent to Zhou for now, and returned when Chezi grows up." Afterward Zhou became immensely wealthy. Learning that once Chezi turned7 or came of age the fortune would revert to him, Zhou loaded his wealth onto carts and fled. One evening he halted by the roadside, and a pregnant servant woman gave birth to a son right beneath his cart; the master named the infant Chezi ("Cart Boy"). From that time on, Zhou's ventures failed and he sank back into poverty as his wealth passed to Chezi.
  • (8) Mount Madang: Wang Bo of the Tang dynasty was traveling south to visit his father at his official post in Jiaozhi. While his boat was moored below Mount Madang, he met an old man who proved to be the spirit of the的中/water realm and promised him a favorable wind. Overnight, a tailwind carried his boat hundreds of li to Nanchang in time for the Double Ninth banquet, where he composed his immortal Preface to the Pavilion of Prince Teng (Tengwang Ge xu).
  • (9) Jianfu stele: Under the Song dynasty, when Fan Zhongyan was governing Raozhou, an impoverished scholar came to call on him and spoke of his hunger and cold. At that time connoisseurs prized rubbings of the calligraphy of Ouyang Xun carved on the stele at Jianfu Temple. Fan prepared paper and ink so the scholar could go to the temple, take a thousand rubbings, and sell them for a handsome sum. That very night, before a single rubbing could be made, a thunderstorm broke and lightning shattered the stele. From this arose the proverb: "Shi lai feng song Tengwang ge, yun qu lei hong Jianfu bei" ("When fortune comes, the wind speeds one to Prince Teng's Pavilion; when luck fails, thunder shatters the Jianfu stele").
  • (10) Yan and Min: Yan Yuan (Yan Hui) and Min Ziqian, two of Confucius's foremost disciples, renowned above all others for their moral virtue.
  • (11) Luo and Lu: Luo Binwang and Lu Zhaolin, two of the "Four Paragons of the Early Tang." The statesman Pei Xingjian remarked that although they possessed brilliant literary gifts, their bearing was restless and lacked the composure of men destined for high rank and longevity. Later, Lu Zhaolin, tormented by chronic illness, drowned himself in the Ying River, while Luo Binwang joined Xu Jingye's rebellion against Empress Wu Zetian and disappeared after its defeat.
  • (12) Truong Giang ("Long/Great River"): Here referring to the Red River (Hong Ha / Nhi Ha).
